[[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]] (brother) | signature = [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune kao.jpg|50px]] }} {{Nihongo|'''Minamoto no Yoshitsune'''|源 義経||{{Circa|1159}} – June 15, 1189}} was a commander of the [[Minamoto clan]] of [[:en:Japan|Japan]] in the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] and early [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura]] periods. During the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], he led a series of battles that toppled the Ise-Heishi branch of the [[Taira clan]], helping his half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo|Yoritomo]] consolidate power. He is considered one of the greatest and the most popular warriors of his era, and one of the most famous [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] in the history of Japan.{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|title=Minamoto Yoshitsune – Japanese warrior|website=britannica.com|access-date=2010-11-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711110631/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|archive-date=2010-07-11|url-status=live}} Yoshitsune perished after being betrayed by the son of a trusted ally and was labelled as a tragic hero. == Early life == [[File:NDL-DC 1302763-Tsukioka Yoshitoshi-芳年武者无類 源牛若丸・熊坂長範-明治16-crd.jpg|thumb|The fight between Ushiwakamaru and the bandit chief [[:en:Kumasaka|Kumasaka]] Chohan in 1174. Yoshitsune was only 15 when he defeated the notorious bandit leader. [[Ukiyo-e]] printed by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. ''Warriors Trembling with Courage ''.|upright=1]] [[File:Yoshitsune aangevallen door Taira geesten-Rijksmuseum RP-P-1979-177.jpeg|thumb|Yoshitsune and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] defending themselves in their boat during a storm created by the ghosts of conquered Taira warriors. Made by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]|upright]] Yoshitsune was the ninth son of [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], and the third and final son and child that Yoshitomo would father with [[Tokiwa Gozen]].{{Cite book |last=Morris |first=Ivan |title=The Nobility of Failure |publisher=Holt, Rinehart and Winston |year=1975 |isbn=978-0-03-010811-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 71–72] |url=https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 }} Yoshitsune's older half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (the third son of Yoshitomo) would go on to establish the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]. Yoshitsune's name in childhood was '''Ushiwakamaru''' or ''young bull'' ({{lang|ja|牛若丸}}). He was born just before the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji rebellion]] in 1160 in which his father and two oldest brothers were killed.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0-8047-0523-2 |pages=258–260, 291}} He survived this incident by fleeing the capital with his mother, while his half-brother Yoritomo was banished to [[:en:Izu Province|Izu Province]]. When he was 10, Yoshitsune was placed in the care of the monks of [[Kurama-dera|Kurama temple]] ({{lang|ja|鞍馬寺}}),{{rp|61}} nestled in the Hiei Mountains near the capital of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. There he was taught swordsmanship and strategy, according to some legends by [[Sōjōbō]], to others by [[:en:Kiichi Hōgen|Kiichi Hōgen]] (whose book, ''[[Six Secret Teachings]]'', Ushiwakamaru stole). Not wanting to become a monk, Yoshitsune eventually left and followed a gold merchant who knew his father well, and in 1174 relocated to [[:en:Hiraizumi, Iwate|Hiraizumi]], [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], where he was put under the protection of [[:en:Fujiwara no Hidehira|Fujiwara no Hidehira]], head of the powerful regional [[:en:Northern Fujiwara|Northern Fujiwara]] clan.{{rp|325}} == Career == [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune,dannoura.jpg|thumb|Statue of Yoshitsune in Mimosusogawa Park, Shimonoseki, near the site of the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]]|upright]] A skillful swordsman, Yoshitsune defeated the legendary warrior monk [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] in a duel. From then on, Benkei became Yoshitsune's retainer, eventually dying with him at the [[:en:Battle of Koromogawa|Siege of Koromogawa]].{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai, A Military History |publisher=MacMillan Publishing Co., Inc. |year=1977 |isbn=0-02-620540-8 |pages=62}} In 1180, Yoshitsune heard that Yoritomo, now head of the Minamoto clan, had raised an army at the request of [[:en:Prince Mochihito|Prince Mochihito]] to fight against the [[Taira clan]] (also known as the Heike) which had usurped the power of the emperor. In the ensuing war between the rival Minamoto and Taira [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] clans, known as the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], Yoshitsune joined Yoritomo, along with [[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]], all brothers who had not previously met. Yoshitsune, together with his brother Noriyori, defeated the Taira in several key battles. He also attacked and killed his cousin [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshinaka|Minamoto no Yoshinaka]], a rival for control of the Minamoto clan, at the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |page=204}} in [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] in early 1184 on the orders of Yoritomo. Yoshitsune, who had by then been given the Rank of general, went on to defeat the Taira at the [[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] in present-day [[:en:Kobe, Hyōgo|Kobe]] in March 1184, and again at the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] in [[Shikoku]] in March 1185. He finally destroyed them one month later at the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] in present-day [[:en:Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi Prefecture]].{{rp|289–305}} Yoshitsune, was then given [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] for him to govern, after the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]. == Final years == Following the Genpei War, Yoshitsune was appointed as Governor of [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo]] and awarded other titles by cloistered emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]].{{Cite book |last=Sato |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator) |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=139}} His suspicious brother Yoritomo, however, opposed the presentation of these titles, and nullified them. [[File:Vase with the Warrior Yoshitsune by Ishikawa Komei.jpg|thumb|An [[:en:ivory carving|ivory carving]] depicting Yoshitsune and his retainers looking at the rough sea while fleeing from Yoritomo's pursuers. by Ishikawa Komei. circa 1880. [[:en:Walters Art Museum|Walters Art Museum]]|upright]] Yoshitsune then secured imperial authorization to ally with his uncle [[:en:Minamoto no Yukiie|Minamoto no Yukiie]] in opposing Yoritomo.{{rp|316}}{{rp|140–143}} Incurring Yoritomo's wrath, Yoshitsune fled Kyoto in 1185. His faithful mistress, [[Shizuka Gozen]], carrying his unborn child, fled with him at first, but then was left behind, and soon taken into custody by forces loyal to Yoritomo. Yoshitsune eventually made his way to Hiraizumi, Mutsu, once again to the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira, and lived undisturbed for a time. Hidehira's son [[:en:Fujiwara no Yasuhira|Fujiwara no Yasuhira]] had promised upon Hidehira's death to honor his father's wishes and continue to shelter Yoshitsune, but, giving in to pressure from Yoritomo, betrayed Yoshitsune, surrounding his Koromogawa-no-tachi residence with his troops, defeating Yoshitsune's retainers, including [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] (in a famous [[Benkei#Death|"standing death"]]), and forcing Yoshitsune to commit [[seppuku]]. Yasuhira then had Yoshitsune's head preserved in sake, placed in a black-lacquered chest, and sent to Yoritomo as proof of his death. Historical sources differ as to the fate of Yoshitsune's mistress Shizuka and their son. Yoshitsune is enshrined in the [[Fujisawa, Kanagawa#Tourist attractions|Shirahata Jinja]], a [[Shinto]] shrine in the city of [[:en:Fujisawa, Kanagawa|Fujisawa]]. == Rumors and legend == The death of Yoshitsune has been very elusive. According to [[:en:Ainu people|Ainu]] historical accounts, he did not commit seppuku, but instead escaped the siege at Koromogawa, fleeing to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and assuming the name Okikurumi/Oinakamui. An alternative legend states that after evading death, Yoshitsune made his way past Hokkaido and sailed to the mainland of Asia, re-surfacing as [[:en:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan]]. This story was invented by [[Suematsu Kenchō]] (1855–1920) while he was studying at [[:en:Cambridge University|Cambridge University]] in 1879, with the aim of improving Japanese prestige in the wake of the [[Meiji Restoration]].{{cite journal |last1=Miyawaki-Okada |first1=Junko |date=2006 |title=The Japanese Origin of the Chinggis Khan Legends |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23615520 |journal=Inner Asia |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=123–134 |doi= 10.1163/146481706793646819|jstor=23615520 |access-date=30 October 2022}} There's a temple Henshoji in [[:en:Mooka, Tochigi|Mooka, Tochigi]]. According to an old temple magazine and tradition, [[Hitachibō Kaison]] entrusted a monk Hitachi Nyūdō Nensai真岡市史案内第4号中村城 真岡市教育委員会発行 栃木県立図書館蔵書 with a child of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Keiwaka, as demanded by Hidehira Fujiwara. Furthermore, according to the tradition of Enmyō-ji temple in [[:en:Hirosaki|Hirosaki]], [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori]], Chitose Maru, also known as Keiwakamaru was a child of Yoshitsune, entrusted to [[:en:Date Tomomune|Date Tomomune]] by Kaison. After the adoption Kaison disappeared.{{citation|title=源義経周辺系図解説|pages=42|author=批評社|year=2016}} == Koshigoe Letter == The "[[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Koshigoe Letter]]" was written by Yoshitsune on the 24th day of the 5th month of the second year of Genryaku (June 23, 1185) as he waited in [[:en:Koshigoe|Koshigoe]] for approval from Yoritomo to enter Kamakura. The letter was Yoshitsune's "final appeal" to Yoritomo of his loyalty. The letter is a "mixture of bravado and an almost masochistic indulgence in misfortune." An excerpt:{{rp|85–86}} {{blockquote | So here I remain, vainly shedding crimson tears....I have not been permitted to refute the accusations of my slanderers or [even] to set foot in Kamakura, but have been obliged to languish idly these many days with no possibility of declaring the sincerity of my intentions. It is now so long since I have set eyes on His Lordship's compassionate countenance that the bond of our blood brotherhood seems to have vanished. }} == In literature == [[File:Yoshitsune with benkei.jpg|thumb|''Yoshitsune and Benkei Viewing Cherry Blossom'', by [[:en:Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi Tsukioka]]|upright]] [[File:Shizuka-gozen in her farewell dance to Yoshitsune.jpg|thumb|Painting of Shizuka Gozen (lady Shizuka) by [[:en:Katsushika Hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] of the most famous shirabyōshi]] Yoshitsune has long been a popular figure in Japanese literature and culture due to his appearance as the main character in the third section of the Japanese literary classic ''[[The Tale of the Heike|Heike Monogatari (Tale of the Heike)]]''. The Japanese term for "sympathy for a tragic hero", {{nihongo|''Hōgan-biiki''|判官贔屓|lit. Hōgan favor}}, comes from Yoshitsune's title ''Kurō Hōgan'' ({{lang|ja|九郎判官}}), which he received from the Imperial Court. Many of the literary pieces that Yoshitsune appears in are legend rather than historical fact. Legends pertaining to Yoshitsune first began to appear in the fourteenth century. In early works at that time, Yoshitsune was described as a sharp-witted military leader.McCullough, Helen. ''Yoshitsune: A Fifteenth-Century Japanese Chronicle''. California: Stanford University Press, 1966. Then, romantic stories about his early childhood and last years of his life appeared as people began to know more about him. The legends that deal with his public career show Yoshitsune as a great, virtuous warrior. He was often shown as kind to those around him and honorable, but was also shown to be naive.{{rp|67,105}} Legends dealing with Yoshitsune's childhood show young Yoshitsune (or Ushiwakamaru) with heroic qualities. He is portrayed as a brave and skilled swordsman, despite being a young boy. He was also skilled in music and his studies, and was also said to be able to easily sway the hearts of young women. These legends delve into fantasy more so than the legends about his later life. Legends which pertain to the time when his half-brother, Yoritomo, turned against him take away some of Yoshitsune's heroic qualities. He is no longer portrayed as a great warrior, but he retains his knowledge and skills that are valuable in the emperor's court. Yoshitsune's escape through the Ataka barrier is the subject of [[:en:Noh|Noh]] play ''[[:en:Ataka (play)|Ataka]]'' and the [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]''.{{rp|89–93}} ''Kanjinchō'' was later dramatized by [[:en:Akira Kurosawa|Akira Kurosawa]] in the 1945 movie ''[[The Men Who Tread on the Tiger's Tail]]''. The ''[[:en:Gikeiki|Gikeiki]]'', or "''Chronicle of Yoshitsune''" relates events of Yoshitsune's life after the defeat of the Heike.{{rp|93–100}} ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] * Mother: [[Tokiwa Gozen]] * Wife: Sato Gozen (1168–1189) * Concubine: [[Shizuka Gozen]] == Traditional arts == In addition to [[The Tale of the Heike]] and ''Gikeiki'', a great many other works of literature and drama feature him, and together form the ''[[sekai and shukō|sekai]]'' ("world") of Yoshitsune, a concept akin to the notion of the [[:en:literary cycle|literary cycle]]. These include: * ''[[Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'') * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura|Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'' and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) * ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]'' ([[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) In the visual arts, Yoshitsune is commonly depicted as a ''[[:en:Bishōnen|Bishōnen]]'', though this is at odds with contemporary descriptions of his appearance. == See also == {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Minamoto no Yoshitsune}} * [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] * [[:en:Kurama-tengu|Kurama-tengu]] * [[:en:Kurozuka (novel)|''Kurozuka'' (novel)]] * [[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Letter from Koshigoe]]{{rp|139}} * ''[[:en:Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II|Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II]]'' * [[:en:Seiwa Genji|Seiwa Genji]] == References == {{Reflist}} == Further reading == * [https://www.illuminationsfantastic.com/the-song-of-yoshitsune-a-story-of-the-gempei-war-duel-at-gojo-bridge-by-alex-j-taylor-japanese-heroes-legend-history-epic-poetry-fantasy-poem-fiction-2021-illuminations-of-the-fantastic-magazine Taylor, Alex J. "The Song of Yoshitsune." Illuminations of the Fantastic Online Magazine. Poetry.] == External links == * [https://web.archive.org/web/20101017230019/http://www.samurai-archives.com/yoshitsune.html Biographical Summary] * {{Cite NIE|wstitle=Minamoto Yoshitsune|year=1905 |short=x}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1150s births]] [[Category:1189 deaths]] [[Category:Deified Japanese men]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese folklore]] [[Category:Japanese legends]] [[Category:Japanese nobility]] [[Category:Kabuki characters]] [[Category:Minamoto clan|Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Nobility from Kyoto]] [[Category:People of Heian-period Japan]] [[Category:People of Kamakura-period Japan]] [[Category:People of the Genpei War]] [[Category:Samurai]] [[Category:Suicides by seppuku]] }} [[sn:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[ar:ميناموتو نو يوشي-تسونه]] [[br:Minamoto no Yoshitune]] [[ca:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[cs:Jošicune Minamoto]] [[de:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[el:Μιναμότο Γιοσιτσούνε]] [[es:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[eu:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fa:میناموتو نو یوشی‌تسونه]] [[fi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[he:מינאמוטו נו יושיצונה]] [[hu:Minamoto no Josicune]] [[hy:Մինամոտո նո Յոշիցունե]] [[id:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[it:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ja:源義経]] [[jv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ko:미나모토노 요시쓰네]] [[lt:Minamoto no Jošicunė]] [[nl:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[pl:Yoshitsune Minamoto]] [[pt:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ru:Минамото-но Ёсицунэ]] [[sq:Minamoto no Joshitsune]] [[sv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[th:มินาโมโตะ โนะ โยชิตสึเนะ]] [[tr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[uk:Мінамото-но Йосіцуне]] [[vi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[wuu:源義經]] [[zh:源義經]] [[zh-min-nan:Minamoto no Yositune]] [[zh-yue:源義經]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]]

In the ensuing war between the rival Minamoto and Taira [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] clans, known as the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], Yoshitsune joined Yoritomo, along with [[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]], all brothers who had not previously met. Yoshitsune, together with his brother Noriyori, defeated the Taira in several key battles. He also attacked and killed his cousin [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshinaka|Minamoto no Yoshinaka]], a rival for control of the Minamoto clan, at the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |page=204}} in [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] in early 1184 on the orders of Yoritomo. Yoshitsune, who had by then been given the Rank of general, went on to defeat the Taira at the [[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] in present-day [[:en:Kobe, Hyōgo|Kobe]] in March 1184, and again at the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] in [[Shikoku]] in March 1185. He finally destroyed them one month later at the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] in present-day [[:en:Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi Prefecture]].{{rp|289–305}} Yoshitsune, was then given [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] for him to govern, after the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]. == Final years == Following the Genpei War, Yoshitsune was appointed as Governor of [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo]] and awarded other titles by cloistered emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]].{{Cite book |last=Sato |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator) |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=139}} His suspicious brother Yoritomo, however, opposed the presentation of these titles, and nullified them. [[File:Vase with the Warrior Yoshitsune by Ishikawa Komei.jpg|thumb|An [[:en:ivory carving|ivory carving]] depicting Yoshitsune and his retainers looking at the rough sea while fleeing from Yoritomo's pursuers. by Ishikawa Komei. circa 1880. [[:en:Walters Art Museum|Walters Art Museum]]|upright]] Yoshitsune then secured imperial authorization to ally with his uncle [[:en:Minamoto no Yukiie|Minamoto no Yukiie]] in opposing Yoritomo.{{rp|316}}{{rp|140–143}} Incurring Yoritomo's wrath, Yoshitsune fled Kyoto in 1185. His faithful mistress, [[Shizuka Gozen]], carrying his unborn child, fled with him at first, but then was left behind, and soon taken into custody by forces loyal to Yoritomo. Yoshitsune eventually made his way to Hiraizumi, Mutsu, once again to the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira, and lived undisturbed for a time. Hidehira's son [[:en:Fujiwara no Yasuhira|Fujiwara no Yasuhira]] had promised upon Hidehira's death to honor his father's wishes and continue to shelter Yoshitsune, but, giving in to pressure from Yoritomo, betrayed Yoshitsune, surrounding his Koromogawa-no-tachi residence with his troops, defeating Yoshitsune's retainers, including [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] (in a famous [[Benkei#Death|"standing death"]]), and forcing Yoshitsune to commit [[seppuku]]. Yasuhira then had Yoshitsune's head preserved in sake, placed in a black-lacquered chest, and sent to Yoritomo as proof of his death. Historical sources differ as to the fate of Yoshitsune's mistress Shizuka and their son. Yoshitsune is enshrined in the [[Fujisawa, Kanagawa#Tourist attractions|Shirahata Jinja]], a [[Shinto]] shrine in the city of [[:en:Fujisawa, Kanagawa|Fujisawa]]. == Rumors and legend == The death of Yoshitsune has been very elusive. According to [[:en:Ainu people|Ainu]] historical accounts, he did not commit seppuku, but instead escaped the siege at Koromogawa, fleeing to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and assuming the name Okikurumi/Oinakamui. An alternative legend states that after evading death, Yoshitsune made his way past Hokkaido and sailed to the mainland of Asia, re-surfacing as [[:en:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan]]. This story was invented by [[Suematsu Kenchō]] (1855–1920) while he was studying at [[:en:Cambridge University|Cambridge University]] in 1879, with the aim of improving Japanese prestige in the wake of the [[Meiji Restoration]].{{cite journal |last1=Miyawaki-Okada |first1=Junko |date=2006 |title=The Japanese Origin of the Chinggis Khan Legends |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23615520 |journal=Inner Asia |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=123–134 |doi= 10.1163/146481706793646819|jstor=23615520 |access-date=30 October 2022}} There's a temple Henshoji in [[:en:Mooka, Tochigi|Mooka, Tochigi]]. According to an old temple magazine and tradition, [[Hitachibō Kaison]] entrusted a monk Hitachi Nyūdō Nensai真岡市史案内第4号中村城 真岡市教育委員会発行 栃木県立図書館蔵書 with a child of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Keiwaka, as demanded by Hidehira Fujiwara. Furthermore, according to the tradition of Enmyō-ji temple in [[:en:Hirosaki|Hirosaki]], [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori]], Chitose Maru, also known as Keiwakamaru was a child of Yoshitsune, entrusted to [[:en:Date Tomomune|Date Tomomune]] by Kaison. After the adoption Kaison disappeared.{{citation|title=源義経周辺系図解説|pages=42|author=批評社|year=2016}} == Koshigoe Letter == The "[[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Koshigoe Letter]]" was written by Yoshitsune on the 24th day of the 5th month of the second year of Genryaku (June 23, 1185) as he waited in [[:en:Koshigoe|Koshigoe]] for approval from Yoritomo to enter Kamakura. The letter was Yoshitsune's "final appeal" to Yoritomo of his loyalty. The letter is a "mixture of bravado and an almost masochistic indulgence in misfortune." An excerpt:{{rp|85–86}} {{blockquote | So here I remain, vainly shedding crimson tears....I have not been permitted to refute the accusations of my slanderers or [even] to set foot in Kamakura, but have been obliged to languish idly these many days with no possibility of declaring the sincerity of my intentions. It is now so long since I have set eyes on His Lordship's compassionate countenance that the bond of our blood brotherhood seems to have vanished. }} == In literature == [[File:Yoshitsune with benkei.jpg|thumb|''Yoshitsune and Benkei Viewing Cherry Blossom'', by [[:en:Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi Tsukioka]]|upright]] [[File:Shizuka-gozen in her farewell dance to Yoshitsune.jpg|thumb|Painting of Shizuka Gozen (lady Shizuka) by [[:en:Katsushika Hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] of the most famous shirabyōshi]] Yoshitsune has long been a popular figure in Japanese literature and culture due to his appearance as the main character in the third section of the Japanese literary classic ''[[The Tale of the Heike|Heike Monogatari (Tale of the Heike)]]''. The Japanese term for "sympathy for a tragic hero", {{nihongo|''Hōgan-biiki''|判官贔屓|lit. Hōgan favor}}, comes from Yoshitsune's title ''Kurō Hōgan'' ({{lang|ja|九郎判官}}), which he received from the Imperial Court. Many of the literary pieces that Yoshitsune appears in are legend rather than historical fact. Legends pertaining to Yoshitsune first began to appear in the fourteenth century. In early works at that time, Yoshitsune was described as a sharp-witted military leader.McCullough, Helen. ''Yoshitsune: A Fifteenth-Century Japanese Chronicle''. California: Stanford University Press, 1966. Then, romantic stories about his early childhood and last years of his life appeared as people began to know more about him. The legends that deal with his public career show Yoshitsune as a great, virtuous warrior. He was often shown as kind to those around him and honorable, but was also shown to be naive.{{rp|67,105}} Legends dealing with Yoshitsune's childhood show young Yoshitsune (or Ushiwakamaru) with heroic qualities. He is portrayed as a brave and skilled swordsman, despite being a young boy. He was also skilled in music and his studies, and was also said to be able to easily sway the hearts of young women. These legends delve into fantasy more so than the legends about his later life. Legends which pertain to the time when his half-brother, Yoritomo, turned against him take away some of Yoshitsune's heroic qualities. He is no longer portrayed as a great warrior, but he retains his knowledge and skills that are valuable in the emperor's court. Yoshitsune's escape through the Ataka barrier is the subject of [[:en:Noh|Noh]] play ''[[:en:Ataka (play)|Ataka]]'' and the [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]''.{{rp|89–93}} ''Kanjinchō'' was later dramatized by [[:en:Akira Kurosawa|Akira Kurosawa]] in the 1945 movie ''[[The Men Who Tread on the Tiger's Tail]]''. The ''[[:en:Gikeiki|Gikeiki]]'', or "''Chronicle of Yoshitsune''" relates events of Yoshitsune's life after the defeat of the Heike.{{rp|93–100}} ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] * Mother: [[Tokiwa Gozen]] * Wife: Sato Gozen (1168–1189) * Concubine: [[Shizuka Gozen]] == Traditional arts == In addition to [[The Tale of the Heike]] and ''Gikeiki'', a great many other works of literature and drama feature him, and together form the ''[[sekai and shukō|sekai]]'' ("world") of Yoshitsune, a concept akin to the notion of the [[:en:literary cycle|literary cycle]]. These include: * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi|Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'') * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura|Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'' and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) * ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]'' ([[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) In the visual arts, Yoshitsune is commonly depicted as a ''[[:en:Bishōnen|Bishōnen]]'', though this is at odds with contemporary descriptions of his appearance. == See also == {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Minamoto no Yoshitsune}} * [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] * [[:en:Kurama-tengu|Kurama-tengu]] * [[:en:Kurozuka (novel)|''Kurozuka'' (novel)]] * [[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Letter from Koshigoe]]{{rp|139}} * ''[[:en:Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II|Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II]]'' * [[:en:Seiwa Genji|Seiwa Genji]] == References == {{Reflist}} == Further reading == * [https://www.illuminationsfantastic.com/the-song-of-yoshitsune-a-story-of-the-gempei-war-duel-at-gojo-bridge-by-alex-j-taylor-japanese-heroes-legend-history-epic-poetry-fantasy-poem-fiction-2021-illuminations-of-the-fantastic-magazine Taylor, Alex J. "The Song of Yoshitsune." Illuminations of the Fantastic Online Magazine. Poetry.] == External links == * [https://web.archive.org/web/20101017230019/http://www.samurai-archives.com/yoshitsune.html Biographical Summary] * {{Cite NIE|wstitle=Minamoto Yoshitsune|year=1905 |short=x}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1150s births]] [[Category:1189 deaths]] [[Category:Deified Japanese men]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese folklore]] [[Category:Japanese legends]] [[Category:Japanese nobility]] [[Category:Kabuki characters]] [[Category:Minamoto clan|Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Nobility from Kyoto]] [[Category:People of Heian-period Japan]] [[Category:People of Kamakura-period Japan]] [[Category:People of the Genpei War]] [[Category:Samurai]] [[Category:Suicides by seppuku]] }} [[sn:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[ar:ميناموتو نو يوشي-تسونه]] [[br:Minamoto no Yoshitune]] [[ca:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[cs:Jošicune Minamoto]] [[de:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[el:Μιναμότο Γιοσιτσούνε]] [[es:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[eu:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fa:میناموتو نو یوشی‌تسونه]] [[fi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[he:מינאמוטו נו יושיצונה]] [[hu:Minamoto no Josicune]] [[hy:Մինամոտո նո Յոշիցունե]] [[id:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[it:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ja:源義経]] [[jv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ko:미나모토노 요시쓰네]] [[lt:Minamoto no Jošicunė]] [[nl:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[pl:Yoshitsune Minamoto]] [[pt:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ru:Минамото-но Ёсицунэ]] [[sq:Minamoto no Joshitsune]] [[sv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[th:มินาโมโตะ โนะ โยชิตสึเนะ]] [[tr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[uk:Мінамото-но Йосіцуне]] [[vi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[wuu:源義經]] [[zh:源義經]] [[zh-min-nan:Minamoto no Yositune]] [[zh-yue:源義經]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]]

[[Tokiwa Gozen]] (mother)
[[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (half-brother)
[[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]] (brother) | signature = [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune kao.jpg|50px]] }} {{Nihongo|'''Minamoto no Yoshitsune'''|源 義経||{{Circa|1159}} – June 15, 1189}} was a commander of the [[Minamoto clan]] of [[:en:Japan|Japan]] in the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] and early [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura]] periods. During the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], he led a series of battles that toppled the Ise-Heishi branch of the [[Taira clan]], helping his half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo|Yoritomo]] consolidate power. He is considered one of the greatest and the most popular warriors of his era, and one of the most famous [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] in the history of Japan.{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|title=Minamoto Yoshitsune – Japanese warrior|website=britannica.com|access-date=2010-11-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711110631/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|archive-date=2010-07-11|url-status=live}} Yoshitsune perished after being betrayed by the son of a trusted ally and was labelled as a tragic hero. == Early life == [[File:NDL-DC 1302763-Tsukioka Yoshitoshi-芳年武者无類 源牛若丸・熊坂長範-明治16-crd.jpg|thumb|The fight between Ushiwakamaru and the bandit chief [[:en:Kumasaka|Kumasaka]] Chohan in 1174. Yoshitsune was only 15 when he defeated the notorious bandit leader. [[Ukiyo-e]] printed by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. ''Warriors Trembling with Courage ''.|upright=1]] [[File:Yoshitsune aangevallen door Taira geesten-Rijksmuseum RP-P-1979-177.jpeg|thumb|Yoshitsune and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] defending themselves in their boat during a storm created by the ghosts of conquered Taira warriors. Made by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]|upright]] Yoshitsune was the ninth son of [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], and the third and final son and child that Yoshitomo would father with [[Tokiwa Gozen]].{{Cite book |last=Morris |first=Ivan |title=The Nobility of Failure |publisher=Holt, Rinehart and Winston |year=1975 |isbn=978-0-03-010811-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 71–72] |url=https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 }} Yoshitsune's older half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (the third son of Yoshitomo) would go on to establish the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]. Yoshitsune's name in childhood was '''Ushiwakamaru''' or ''young bull'' ({{lang|ja|牛若丸}}). He was born just before the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji rebellion]] in 1160 in which his father and two oldest brothers were killed.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0-8047-0523-2 |pages=258–260, 291}} He survived this incident by fleeing the capital with his mother, while his half-brother Yoritomo was banished to [[:en:Izu Province|Izu Province]]. When he was 10, Yoshitsune was placed in the care of the monks of [[Kurama-dera|Kurama temple]] ({{lang|ja|鞍馬寺}}),{{rp|61}} nestled in the Hiei Mountains near the capital of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. There he was taught swordsmanship and strategy, according to some legends by [[Sōjōbō]], to others by [[:en:Kiichi Hōgen|Kiichi Hōgen]] (whose book, ''[[Six Secret Teachings]]'', Ushiwakamaru stole). Not wanting to become a monk, Yoshitsune eventually left and followed a gold merchant who knew his father well, and in 1174 relocated to [[:en:Hiraizumi, Iwate|Hiraizumi]], [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], where he was put under the protection of [[:en:Fujiwara no Hidehira|Fujiwara no Hidehira]], head of the powerful regional [[:en:Northern Fujiwara|Northern Fujiwara]] clan.{{rp|325}} == Career == [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune,dannoura.jpg|thumb|Statue of Yoshitsune in Mimosusogawa Park, Shimonoseki, near the site of the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]]|upright]] A skillful swordsman, Yoshitsune defeated the legendary warrior monk [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] in a duel. From then on, Benkei became Yoshitsune's retainer, eventually dying with him at the [[:en:Battle of Koromogawa|Siege of Koromogawa]].{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai, A Military History |publisher=MacMillan Publishing Co., Inc. |year=1977 |isbn=0-02-620540-8 |pages=62}} In 1180, Yoshitsune heard that Yoritomo, now head of the Minamoto clan, had raised an army at the request of [[:en:Prince Mochihito|Prince Mochihito]] to fight against the [[Taira clan]] (also known as the Heike) which had usurped the power of the emperor. In the ensuing war between the rival Minamoto and Taira [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] clans, known as the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], Yoshitsune joined Yoritomo, along with [[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]], all brothers who had not previously met. Yoshitsune, together with his brother Noriyori, defeated the Taira in several key battles. He also attacked and killed his cousin [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshinaka|Minamoto no Yoshinaka]], a rival for control of the Minamoto clan, at the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |page=204}} in [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] in early 1184 on the orders of Yoritomo. Yoshitsune, who had by then been given the Rank of general, went on to defeat the Taira at the [[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] in present-day [[:en:Kobe, Hyōgo|Kobe]] in March 1184, and again at the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] in [[Shikoku]] in March 1185. He finally destroyed them one month later at the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] in present-day [[:en:Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi Prefecture]].{{rp|289–305}} Yoshitsune, was then given [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] for him to govern, after the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]. == Final years == Following the Genpei War, Yoshitsune was appointed as Governor of [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo]] and awarded other titles by cloistered emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]].{{Cite book |last=Sato |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator) |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=139}} His suspicious brother Yoritomo, however, opposed the presentation of these titles, and nullified them. [[File:Vase with the Warrior Yoshitsune by Ishikawa Komei.jpg|thumb|An [[:en:ivory carving|ivory carving]] depicting Yoshitsune and his retainers looking at the rough sea while fleeing from Yoritomo's pursuers. by Ishikawa Komei. circa 1880. [[:en:Walters Art Museum|Walters Art Museum]]|upright]] Yoshitsune then secured imperial authorization to ally with his uncle [[:en:Minamoto no Yukiie|Minamoto no Yukiie]] in opposing Yoritomo.{{rp|316}}{{rp|140–143}} Incurring Yoritomo's wrath, Yoshitsune fled Kyoto in 1185. Yoshitsune eventually made his way to Hiraizumi, Mutsu, once again to the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira, and lived undisturbed for a time. Hidehira's son [[:en:Fujiwara no Yasuhira|Fujiwara no Yasuhira]] had promised upon Hidehira's death to honor his father's wishes and continue to shelter Yoshitsune, but, giving in to pressure from Yoritomo, betrayed Yoshitsune, surrounding his Koromogawa-no-tachi residence with his troops, defeating Yoshitsune's retainers, including [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] (in a famous [[Benkei#Death|"standing death"]]), and forcing Yoshitsune to commit [[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]. Furthermore, according to the tradition of Enmyō-ji temple in [[:en:Hirosaki|Hirosaki]], [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori]], Chitose Maru, also known as Keiwakamaru was a child of Yoshitsune, entrusted to [[:en:Date Tomomune|Date Tomomune]] by Kaison. After the adoption Kaison disappeared.{{citation|title=源義経周辺系図解説|pages=42|author=批評社|year=2016}} == Koshigoe Letter == The "[[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Koshigoe Letter]]" was written by Yoshitsune on the 24th day of the 5th month of the second year of Genryaku (June 23, 1185) as he waited in [[:en:Koshigoe|Koshigoe]] for approval from Yoritomo to enter Kamakura. The letter was Yoshitsune's "final appeal" to Yoritomo of his loyalty. The letter is a "mixture of bravado and an almost masochistic indulgence in misfortune." An excerpt:{{rp|85–86}} {{blockquote | So here I remain, vainly shedding crimson tears....I have not been permitted to refute the accusations of my slanderers or [even] to set foot in Kamakura, but have been obliged to languish idly these many days with no possibility of declaring the sincerity of my intentions. It is now so long since I have set eyes on His Lordship's compassionate countenance that the bond of our blood brotherhood seems to have vanished. }} == In literature == [[File:Yoshitsune with benkei.jpg|thumb|''Yoshitsune and Benkei Viewing Cherry Blossom'', by [[:en:Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi Tsukioka]]|upright]] [[File:Shizuka-gozen in her farewell dance to Yoshitsune.jpg|thumb|Painting of Shizuka Gozen (lady Shizuka) by [[:en:Katsushika Hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] of the most famous shirabyōshi]] Yoshitsune has long been a popular figure in Japanese literature and culture due to his appearance as the main character in the third section of the Japanese literary classic ''[[The Tale of the Heike|Heike Monogatari (Tale of the Heike)]]''. The Japanese term for "sympathy for a tragic hero", {{nihongo|''Hōgan-biiki''|判官贔屓|lit. Hōgan favor}}, comes from Yoshitsune's title ''Kurō Hōgan'' ({{lang|ja|九郎判官}}), which he received from the Imperial Court. Many of the literary pieces that Yoshitsune appears in are legend rather than historical fact. Legends pertaining to Yoshitsune first began to appear in the fourteenth century. In early works at that time, Yoshitsune was described as a sharp-witted military leader.McCullough, Helen. ''Yoshitsune: A Fifteenth-Century Japanese Chronicle''. California: Stanford University Press, 1966. Then, romantic stories about his early childhood and last years of his life appeared as people began to know more about him. The legends that deal with his public career show Yoshitsune as a great, virtuous warrior. He was often shown as kind to those around him and honorable, but was also shown to be naive.{{rp|67,105}} Legends dealing with Yoshitsune's childhood show young Yoshitsune (or Ushiwakamaru) with heroic qualities. He is portrayed as a brave and skilled swordsman, despite being a young boy. He was also skilled in music and his studies, and was also said to be able to easily sway the hearts of young women. These legends delve into fantasy more so than the legends about his later life. Legends which pertain to the time when his half-brother, Yoritomo, turned against him take away some of Yoshitsune's heroic qualities. He is no longer portrayed as a great warrior, but he retains his knowledge and skills that are valuable in the emperor's court. Yoshitsune's escape through the Ataka barrier is the subject of [[:en:Noh|Noh]] play ''[[:en:Ataka (play)|Ataka]]'' and the [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]''.{{rp|89–93}} ''Kanjinchō'' was later dramatized by [[:en:Akira Kurosawa|Akira Kurosawa]] in the 1945 movie ''[[The Men Who Tread on the Tiger's Tail]]''. The ''[[:en:Gikeiki|Gikeiki]]'', or "''Chronicle of Yoshitsune''" relates events of Yoshitsune's life after the defeat of the Heike.{{rp|93–100}} ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] * Mother: [[Tokiwa Gozen]] * Wife: Sato Gozen (1168–1189) * Concubine: [[Shizuka Gozen]] == Traditional arts == In addition to [[The Tale of the Heike]] and ''Gikeiki'', a great many other works of literature and drama feature him, and together form the ''[[sekai and shukō|sekai]]'' ("world") of Yoshitsune, a concept akin to the notion of the [[:en:literary cycle|literary cycle]]. These include: * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi|Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'') * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura|Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'' and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) * ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]'' ([[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) In the visual arts, Yoshitsune is commonly depicted as a ''[[:en:Bishōnen|Bishōnen]]'', though this is at odds with contemporary descriptions of his appearance. == See also == {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Minamoto no Yoshitsune}} * [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] * [[:en:Kurama-tengu|Kurama-tengu]] * [[:en:Kurozuka (novel)|''Kurozuka'' (novel)]] * [[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Letter from Koshigoe]]{{rp|139}} * ''[[:en:Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II|Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II]]'' * [[:en:Seiwa Genji|Seiwa Genji]] == References == {{Reflist}} == Further reading == * [https://www.illuminationsfantastic.com/the-song-of-yoshitsune-a-story-of-the-gempei-war-duel-at-gojo-bridge-by-alex-j-taylor-japanese-heroes-legend-history-epic-poetry-fantasy-poem-fiction-2021-illuminations-of-the-fantastic-magazine Taylor, Alex J. "The Song of Yoshitsune." Illuminations of the Fantastic Online Magazine. Poetry.] == External links == * [https://web.archive.org/web/20101017230019/http://www.samurai-archives.com/yoshitsune.html Biographical Summary] * {{Cite NIE|wstitle=Minamoto Yoshitsune|year=1905 |short=x}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1150s births]] [[Category:1189 deaths]] [[Category:Deified Japanese men]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese folklore]] [[Category:Japanese legends]] [[Category:Japanese nobility]] [[Category:Kabuki characters]] [[Category:Minamoto clan|Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Nobility from Kyoto]] [[Category:People of Heian-period Japan]] [[Category:People of Kamakura-period Japan]] [[Category:People of the Genpei War]] [[Category:Samurai]] [[Category:Suicides by seppuku]] }} [[sn:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[ar:ميناموتو نو يوشي-تسونه]] [[br:Minamoto no Yoshitune]] [[ca:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[cs:Jošicune Minamoto]] [[de:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[el:Μιναμότο Γιοσιτσούνε]] [[es:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[eu:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fa:میناموتو نو یوشی‌تسونه]] [[fi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[he:מינאמוטו נו יושיצונה]] [[hu:Minamoto no Josicune]] [[hy:Մինամոտո նո Յոշիցունե]] [[id:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[it:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ja:源義経]] [[jv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ko:미나모토노 요시쓰네]] [[lt:Minamoto no Jošicunė]] [[nl:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[pl:Yoshitsune Minamoto]] [[pt:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ru:Минамото-но Ёсицунэ]] [[sq:Minamoto no Joshitsune]] [[sv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[th:มินาโมโตะ โนะ โยชิตสึเนะ]] [[tr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[uk:Мінамото-но Йосіцуне]] [[vi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[wuu:源義經]] [[zh:源義經]] [[zh-min-nan:Minamoto no Yositune]] [[zh-yue:源義經]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]]

{{Short description|12th-century military commander in the Minamoto clan of feudal Japan}} {{family name hatnote|Minamoto|lang=Japanese}}{{Infobox military person | name = Minamoto Yoshitsune | native_name = 源 義経 | native_name_lang = [[Japanese]] | image = Minamoto_no_Yoshitsune.jpg | caption = Portrait of Yoshitsune in the Chusonji collection | birth_date = Ushiwakamaru (牛若丸)
{{Circa|1159}} | birth_place = [[:en:Heian-kyō|Heian-kyō]], Heian Japan | death_date = June 15, 1189 (aged 30) | death_place = [[:en:Battle of Koromo River|Battle of Koromo River]]
[[:en:Hiraizumi|Hiraizumi]], [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]] | branch = [[Minamoto clan|Minamoto]] | branch_label = Family | battles = [[:en:Battle of Uji (1184)|Battle of Uji]] (1184)
[[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]] (1184)
[[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] (1184)
[[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] (1185)
[[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] (1185)
[[:en:Battle of Koromo River|Battle of Koromo River]] (1189) | spouse = Sato Gozen | relations = [[Shizuka Gozen]] (concubine)
[[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] (father)
[[Tokiwa Gozen]] (mother)
[[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (half-brother)
[[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]] (brother) | signature = [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune kao.jpg|50px]] }} {{Nihongo|'''Minamoto no Yoshitsune'''|源 義経||{{Circa|1159}} – June 15, 1189}} was a commander of the [[Minamoto clan]] of [[:en:Japan|Japan]] in the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] and early [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura]] periods. During the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], he led a series of battles that toppled the Ise-Heishi branch of the [[Taira clan]], helping his half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo|Yoritomo]] consolidate power. He is considered one of the greatest and the most popular warriors of his era, and one of the most famous [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] in the history of Japan.{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|title=Minamoto Yoshitsune – Japanese warrior|website=britannica.com|access-date=2010-11-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711110631/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|archive-date=2010-07-11|url-status=live}} Yoshitsune perished after being betrayed by the son of a trusted ally and was labelled as a tragic hero. == Early life == [[File:NDL-DC 1302763-Tsukioka Yoshitoshi-芳年武者无類 源牛若丸・熊坂長範-明治16-crd.jpg|thumb|The fight between Ushiwakamaru and the bandit chief [[:en:Kumasaka|Kumasaka]] Chohan in 1174. Yoshitsune was only 15 when he defeated the notorious bandit leader. [[Ukiyo-e]] printed by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. ''Warriors Trembling with Courage ''.|upright=1]] [[File:Yoshitsune aangevallen door Taira geesten-Rijksmuseum RP-P-1979-177.jpeg|thumb|Yoshitsune and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] defending themselves in their boat during a storm created by the ghosts of conquered Taira warriors. Made by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]|upright]] Yoshitsune was the ninth son of [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], and the third and final son and child that Yoshitomo would father with [[Tokiwa Gozen]].{{Cite book |last=Morris |first=Ivan |title=The Nobility of Failure |publisher=Holt, Rinehart and Winston |year=1975 |isbn=978-0-03-010811-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 71–72] |url=https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 }} Yoshitsune's older half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (the third son of Yoshitomo) would go on to establish the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]. Yoshitsune's name in childhood was '''Ushiwakamaru''' or ''young bull'' ({{lang|ja|牛若丸}}). He was born just before the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji rebellion]] in 1160 in which his father and two oldest brothers were killed.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0-8047-0523-2 |pages=258–260, 291}} He survived this incident by fleeing the capital with his mother, while his half-brother Yoritomo was banished to [[:en:Izu Province|Izu Province]]. When he was 10, Yoshitsune was placed in the care of the monks of [[Kurama-dera|Kurama temple]] ({{lang|ja|鞍馬寺}}),{{rp|61}} nestled in the Hiei Mountains near the capital of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. There he was taught swordsmanship and strategy, according to some legends by [[Sōjōbō]], to others by [[:en:Kiichi Hōgen|Kiichi Hōgen]] (whose book, ''[[Six Secret Teachings]]'', Ushiwakamaru stole). Not wanting to become a monk, Yoshitsune eventually left and followed a gold merchant who knew his father well, and in 1174 relocated to [[:en:Hiraizumi, Iwate|Hiraizumi]], [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], where he was put under the protection of [[:en:Fujiwara no Hidehira|Fujiwara no Hidehira]], head of the powerful regional [[:en:Northern Fujiwara|Northern Fujiwara]] clan.{{rp|325}} == Career == [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune,dannoura.jpg|thumb|Statue of Yoshitsune in Mimosusogawa Park, Shimonoseki, near the site of the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]]|upright]] A skillful swordsman, Yoshitsune defeated the legendary warrior monk [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] in a duel. From then on, Benkei became Yoshitsune's retainer, eventually dying with him at the [[:en:Battle of Koromogawa|Siege of Koromogawa]].{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai, A Military History |publisher=MacMillan Publishing Co., Inc. |year=1977 |isbn=0-02-620540-8 |pages=62}} In 1180, Yoshitsune heard that Yoritomo, now head of the Minamoto clan, had raised an army at the request of [[:en:Prince Mochihito|Prince Mochihito]] to fight against the [[Taira clan]] (also known as the Heike) which had usurped the power of the emperor. In the ensuing war between the rival Minamoto and Taira [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] clans, known as the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], Yoshitsune joined Yoritomo, along with [[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]], all brothers who had not previously met. Yoshitsune, together with his brother Noriyori, defeated the Taira in several key battles. He also attacked and killed his cousin [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshinaka|Minamoto no Yoshinaka]], a rival for control of the Minamoto clan, at the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |page=204}} in [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] in early 1184 on the orders of Yoritomo. Yoshitsune, who had by then been given the Rank of general, went on to defeat the Taira at the [[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] in present-day [[:en:Kobe, Hyōgo|Kobe]] in March 1184, and again at the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] in [[Shikoku]] in March 1185. He finally destroyed them one month later at the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] in present-day [[:en:Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi Prefecture]].{{rp|289–305}} Yoshitsune, was then given [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] for him to govern, after the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]. == Final years == Following the Genpei War, Yoshitsune was appointed as Governor of [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo]] and awarded other titles by cloistered emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]].{{Cite book |last=Sato |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator) |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=139}} His suspicious brother Yoritomo, however, opposed the presentation of these titles, and nullified them. [[File:Vase with the Warrior Yoshitsune by Ishikawa Komei.jpg|thumb|An [[:en:ivory carving|ivory carving]] depicting Yoshitsune and his retainers looking at the rough sea while fleeing from Yoritomo's pursuers. by Ishikawa Komei. circa 1880. [[:en:Walters Art Museum|Walters Art Museum]]|upright]] Yoshitsune then secured imperial authorization to ally with his uncle [[:en:Minamoto no Yukiie|Minamoto no Yukiie]] in opposing Yoritomo.{{rp|316}}{{rp|140–143}} Incurring Yoritomo's wrath, Yoshitsune fled Kyoto in 1185. His faithful mistress, [[Shizuka Gozen]], carrying his unborn child, fled with him at first, but then was left behind, and soon taken into custody by forces loyal to Yoritomo. Yoshitsune eventually made his way to Hiraizumi, Mutsu, once again to the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira, and lived undisturbed for a time. Hidehira's son [[:en:Fujiwara no Yasuhira|Fujiwara no Yasuhira]] had promised upon Hidehira's death to honor his father's wishes and continue to shelter Yoshitsune, but, giving in to pressure from Yoritomo, betrayed Yoshitsune, surrounding his Koromogawa-no-tachi residence with his troops, defeating Yoshitsune's retainers, including [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] (in a famous [[Benkei#Death|"standing death"]]), and forcing Yoshitsune to commit [[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]. Yasuhira then had Yoshitsune's head preserved in sake, placed in a black-lacquered chest, and sent to Yoritomo as proof of his death. Historical sources differ as to the fate of Yoshitsune's mistress Shizuka and their son. Yoshitsune is enshrined in the [[Fujisawa, Kanagawa#Tourist attractions|Shirahata Jinja]], a [[Shinto]] shrine in the city of [[:en:Fujisawa, Kanagawa|Fujisawa]]. == Rumors and legend == The death of Yoshitsune has been very elusive. According to [[:en:Ainu people|Ainu]] historical accounts, he did not commit seppuku, but instead escaped the siege at Koromogawa, fleeing to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and assuming the name Okikurumi/Oinakamui. An alternative legend states that after evading death, Yoshitsune made his way past Hokkaido and sailed to the mainland of Asia, re-surfacing as [[:en:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan]]. This story was invented by [[:en:Suematsu Kenchō|Suematsu Kenchō]] (1855–1920) while he was studying at [[:en:Cambridge University|Cambridge University]] in 1879, with the aim of improving Japanese prestige in the wake of the [[Meiji Restoration]].{{cite journal |last1=Miyawaki-Okada |first1=Junko |date=2006 |title=The Japanese Origin of the Chinggis Khan Legends |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23615520 |journal=Inner Asia |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=123–134 |doi= 10.1163/146481706793646819|jstor=23615520 |access-date=30 October 2022}} There's a temple Henshoji in [[:en:Mooka, Tochigi|Mooka, Tochigi]]. According to an old temple magazine and tradition, [[Hitachibō Kaison]] entrusted a monk Hitachi Nyūdō Nensai真岡市史案内第4号中村城 真岡市教育委員会発行 栃木県立図書館蔵書 with a child of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Keiwaka, as demanded by Hidehira Fujiwara. Furthermore, according to the tradition of Enmyō-ji temple in [[:en:Hirosaki|Hirosaki]], [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori]], Chitose Maru, also known as Keiwakamaru was a child of Yoshitsune, entrusted to [[:en:Date Tomomune|Date Tomomune]] by Kaison. After the adoption Kaison disappeared.{{citation|title=源義経周辺系図解説|pages=42|author=批評社|year=2016}} == Koshigoe Letter == The "[[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Koshigoe Letter]]" was written by Yoshitsune on the 24th day of the 5th month of the second year of Genryaku (June 23, 1185) as he waited in [[:en:Koshigoe|Koshigoe]] for approval from Yoritomo to enter Kamakura. The letter was Yoshitsune's "final appeal" to Yoritomo of his loyalty. The letter is a "mixture of bravado and an almost masochistic indulgence in misfortune." An excerpt:{{rp|85–86}} {{blockquote | So here I remain, vainly shedding crimson tears....I have not been permitted to refute the accusations of my slanderers or [even] to set foot in Kamakura, but have been obliged to languish idly these many days with no possibility of declaring the sincerity of my intentions. It is now so long since I have set eyes on His Lordship's compassionate countenance that the bond of our blood brotherhood seems to have vanished. }} == In literature == [[File:Yoshitsune with benkei.jpg|thumb|''Yoshitsune and Benkei Viewing Cherry Blossom'', by [[:en:Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi Tsukioka]]|upright]] [[File:Shizuka-gozen in her farewell dance to Yoshitsune.jpg|thumb|Painting of Shizuka Gozen (lady Shizuka) by [[:en:Katsushika Hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] of the most famous shirabyōshi]] Yoshitsune has long been a popular figure in Japanese literature and culture due to his appearance as the main character in the third section of the Japanese literary classic ''[[The Tale of the Heike|Heike Monogatari (Tale of the Heike)]]''. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (half-brother)
[[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]] (brother) | signature = [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune kao.jpg|50px]] }} {{Nihongo|'''Minamoto no Yoshitsune'''|源 義経||{{Circa|1159}} – June 15, 1189}} was a commander of the [[Minamoto clan]] of [[:en:Japan|Japan]] in the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] and early [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura]] periods. During the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], he led a series of battles that toppled the Ise-Heishi branch of the [[Taira clan]], helping his half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo|Yoritomo]] consolidate power. He is considered one of the greatest and the most popular warriors of his era, and one of the most famous [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] in the history of Japan.{{cite web|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|title=Minamoto Yoshitsune – Japanese warrior|website=britannica.com|access-date=2010-11-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100711110631/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/383453/Minamoto-Yoshitsune|archive-date=2010-07-11|url-status=live}} Yoshitsune perished after being betrayed by the son of a trusted ally and was labelled as a tragic hero. == Early life == [[File:NDL-DC 1302763-Tsukioka Yoshitoshi-芳年武者无類 源牛若丸・熊坂長範-明治16-crd.jpg|thumb|The fight between Ushiwakamaru and the bandit chief [[:en:Kumasaka|Kumasaka]] Chohan in 1174. Yoshitsune was only 15 when he defeated the notorious bandit leader. [[Ukiyo-e]] printed by [[Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]]. ''Warriors Trembling with Courage ''.|upright=1]] [[File:Yoshitsune aangevallen door Taira geesten-Rijksmuseum RP-P-1979-177.jpeg|thumb|Yoshitsune and [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] defending themselves in their boat during a storm created by the ghosts of conquered Taira warriors. Made by [[Utagawa Kuniyoshi]]|upright]] Yoshitsune was the ninth son of [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]], and the third and final son and child that Yoshitomo would father with [[Tokiwa Gozen]].{{Cite book |last=Morris |first=Ivan |title=The Nobility of Failure |publisher=Holt, Rinehart and Winston |year=1975 |isbn=978-0-03-010811-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 71–72] |url=https://archive.org/details/nobilityoffailur00morr/page/71 }} Yoshitsune's older half-brother [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] (the third son of Yoshitomo) would go on to establish the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]. Yoshitsune's name in childhood was '''Ushiwakamaru''' or ''young bull'' ({{lang|ja|牛若丸}}). He was born just before the [[:en:Heiji rebellion|Heiji rebellion]] in 1160 in which his father and two oldest brothers were killed.{{Cite book |last=Sansom |first=George |title=A History of Japan to 1334 |publisher=Stanford University Press |year=1958 |isbn=0-8047-0523-2 |pages=258–260, 291}} He survived this incident by fleeing the capital with his mother, while his half-brother Yoritomo was banished to [[:en:Izu Province|Izu Province]]. When he was 10, Yoshitsune was placed in the care of the monks of [[Kurama-dera|Kurama temple]] ({{lang|ja|鞍馬寺}}),{{rp|61}} nestled in the Hiei Mountains near the capital of [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. There he was taught swordsmanship and strategy, according to some legends by [[Sōjōbō]], to others by [[:en:Kiichi Hōgen|Kiichi Hōgen]] (whose book, ''[[Six Secret Teachings]]'', Ushiwakamaru stole). Not wanting to become a monk, Yoshitsune eventually left and followed a gold merchant who knew his father well, and in 1174 relocated to [[:en:Hiraizumi, Iwate|Hiraizumi]], [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], where he was put under the protection of [[:en:Fujiwara no Hidehira|Fujiwara no Hidehira]], head of the powerful regional [[:en:Northern Fujiwara|Northern Fujiwara]] clan.{{rp|325}} == Career == [[File:Minamoto no Yoshitsune,dannoura.jpg|thumb|Statue of Yoshitsune in Mimosusogawa Park, Shimonoseki, near the site of the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]]|upright]] A skillful swordsman, Yoshitsune defeated the legendary warrior monk [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] in a duel. From then on, Benkei became Yoshitsune's retainer, eventually dying with him at the [[:en:Battle of Koromogawa|Siege of Koromogawa]].{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai, A Military History |publisher=MacMillan Publishing Co., Inc. |year=1977 |isbn=0-02-620540-8 |pages=62}} In 1180, Yoshitsune heard that Yoritomo, now head of the Minamoto clan, had raised an army at the request of [[:en:Prince Mochihito|Prince Mochihito]] to fight against the [[Taira clan]] (also known as the Heike) which had usurped the power of the emperor. In the ensuing war between the rival Minamoto and Taira [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] clans, known as the [[:en:Genpei War|Genpei War]], Yoshitsune joined Yoritomo, along with [[:en:Minamoto no Noriyori|Minamoto no Noriyori]], all brothers who had not previously met. Yoshitsune, together with his brother Noriyori, defeated the Taira in several key battles. He also attacked and killed his cousin [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshinaka|Minamoto no Yoshinaka]], a rival for control of the Minamoto clan, at the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]{{Cite book |last=Turnbull |first=Stephen |title=The Samurai Sourcebook |publisher=Cassell & Co. |year=1998 |isbn=1-85409-523-4 |page=204}} in [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] in early 1184 on the orders of Yoritomo. Yoshitsune, who had by then been given the Rank of general, went on to defeat the Taira at the [[:en:Battle of Ichi-no-Tani|Battle of Ichi-no-Tani]] in present-day [[:en:Kobe, Hyōgo|Kobe]] in March 1184, and again at the [[:en:Battle of Yashima|Battle of Yashima]] in [[Shikoku]] in March 1185. He finally destroyed them one month later at the [[:en:Battle of Dan-no-ura|Battle of Dan-no-ura]] in present-day [[:en:Yamaguchi Prefecture|Yamaguchi Prefecture]].{{rp|289–305}} Yoshitsune, was then given [[:en:Ōmi Province|Ōmi Province]] for him to govern, after the [[:en:Battle of Awazu|Battle of Awazu]]. == Final years == Following the Genpei War, Yoshitsune was appointed as Governor of [[:en:Iyo Province|Iyo]] and awarded other titles by cloistered emperor [[:en:Emperor Go-Shirakawa|Go-Shirakawa]].{{Cite book |last=Sato |author-link=Hiroaki Sato (translator) |first=Hiroaki |title=Legends of the Samurai |publisher=Overlook Duckworth |year=1995 |isbn=978-1-59020-730-7 |page=139}} His suspicious brother Yoritomo, however, opposed the presentation of these titles, and nullified them. [[File:Vase with the Warrior Yoshitsune by Ishikawa Komei.jpg|thumb|An [[:en:ivory carving|ivory carving]] depicting Yoshitsune and his retainers looking at the rough sea while fleeing from Yoritomo's pursuers. by Ishikawa Komei. circa 1880. [[:en:Walters Art Museum|Walters Art Museum]]|upright]] Yoshitsune then secured imperial authorization to ally with his uncle [[:en:Minamoto no Yukiie|Minamoto no Yukiie]] in opposing Yoritomo.{{rp|316}}{{rp|140–143}} Incurring Yoritomo's wrath, Yoshitsune fled Kyoto in 1185. His faithful mistress, [[Shizuka Gozen]], carrying his unborn child, fled with him at first, but then was left behind, and soon taken into custody by forces loyal to Yoritomo. Yoshitsune eventually made his way to Hiraizumi, Mutsu, once again to the protection of Fujiwara no Hidehira, and lived undisturbed for a time. Hidehira's son [[:en:Fujiwara no Yasuhira|Fujiwara no Yasuhira]] had promised upon Hidehira's death to honor his father's wishes and continue to shelter Yoshitsune, but, giving in to pressure from Yoritomo, betrayed Yoshitsune, surrounding his Koromogawa-no-tachi residence with his troops, defeating Yoshitsune's retainers, including [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] (in a famous [[Benkei#Death|"standing death"]]), and forcing Yoshitsune to commit [[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]. Yasuhira then had Yoshitsune's head preserved in sake, placed in a black-lacquered chest, and sent to Yoritomo as proof of his death. Historical sources differ as to the fate of Yoshitsune's mistress Shizuka and their son. Yoshitsune is enshrined in the [[Fujisawa, Kanagawa#Tourist attractions|Shirahata Jinja]], a [[Shinto]] shrine in the city of [[:en:Fujisawa, Kanagawa|Fujisawa]]. == Rumors and legend == The death of Yoshitsune has been very elusive. According to [[:en:Ainu people|Ainu]] historical accounts, he did not commit seppuku, but instead escaped the siege at Koromogawa, fleeing to [[:en:Hokkaidō|Hokkaidō]] and assuming the name Okikurumi/Oinakamui. An alternative legend states that after evading death, Yoshitsune made his way past Hokkaido and sailed to the mainland of Asia, re-surfacing as [[:en:Genghis Khan|Genghis Khan]]. This story was invented by [[:en:Suematsu Kenchō|Suematsu Kenchō]] (1855–1920) while he was studying at [[:en:Cambridge University|Cambridge University]] in 1879, with the aim of improving Japanese prestige in the wake of the [[Meiji Restoration]].{{cite journal |last1=Miyawaki-Okada |first1=Junko |date=2006 |title=The Japanese Origin of the Chinggis Khan Legends |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23615520 |journal=Inner Asia |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=123–134 |doi= 10.1163/146481706793646819|jstor=23615520 |access-date=30 October 2022}} There's a temple Henshoji in [[:en:Mooka, Tochigi|Mooka, Tochigi]]. According to an old temple magazine and tradition, [[Hitachibō Kaison]] entrusted a monk Hitachi Nyūdō Nensai真岡市史案内第4号中村城 真岡市教育委員会発行 栃木県立図書館蔵書 with a child of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, Keiwaka, as demanded by Hidehira Fujiwara. Furthermore, according to the tradition of Enmyō-ji temple in [[:en:Hirosaki|Hirosaki]], [[:en:Aomori Prefecture|Aomori]], Chitose Maru, also known as Keiwakamaru was a child of Yoshitsune, entrusted to [[:en:Date Tomomune|Date Tomomune]] by Kaison. After the adoption Kaison disappeared.{{citation|title=源義経周辺系図解説|pages=42|author=批評社|year=2016}} == Koshigoe Letter == The "[[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Koshigoe Letter]]" was written by Yoshitsune on the 24th day of the 5th month of the second year of Genryaku (June 23, 1185) as he waited in [[:en:Koshigoe|Koshigoe]] for approval from Yoritomo to enter Kamakura. The letter was Yoshitsune's "final appeal" to Yoritomo of his loyalty. The letter is a "mixture of bravado and an almost masochistic indulgence in misfortune." An excerpt:{{rp|85–86}} {{blockquote | So here I remain, vainly shedding crimson tears....I have not been permitted to refute the accusations of my slanderers or [even] to set foot in Kamakura, but have been obliged to languish idly these many days with no possibility of declaring the sincerity of my intentions. It is now so long since I have set eyes on His Lordship's compassionate countenance that the bond of our blood brotherhood seems to have vanished. }} == In literature == [[File:Yoshitsune with benkei.jpg|thumb|''Yoshitsune and Benkei Viewing Cherry Blossom'', by [[:en:Yoshitoshi|Yoshitoshi Tsukioka]]|upright]] [[File:Shizuka-gozen in her farewell dance to Yoshitsune.jpg|thumb|Painting of Shizuka Gozen (lady Shizuka) by [[:en:Katsushika Hokusai|Katsushika Hokusai]] of the most famous shirabyōshi]] Yoshitsune has long been a popular figure in Japanese literature and culture due to his appearance as the main character in the third section of the Japanese literary classic ''[[The Tale of the Heike|Heike Monogatari (Tale of the Heike)]]''. The Japanese term for "sympathy for a tragic hero", {{nihongo|''Hōgan-biiki''|判官贔屓|lit. Hōgan favor}}, comes from Yoshitsune's title ''Kurō Hōgan'' ({{lang|ja|九郎判官}}), which he received from the Imperial Court. Many of the literary pieces that Yoshitsune appears in are legend rather than historical fact. Legends pertaining to Yoshitsune first began to appear in the fourteenth century. In early works at that time, Yoshitsune was described as a sharp-witted military leader.McCullough, Helen. ''Yoshitsune: A Fifteenth-Century Japanese Chronicle''. California: Stanford University Press, 1966. Then, romantic stories about his early childhood and last years of his life appeared as people began to know more about him. The legends that deal with his public career show Yoshitsune as a great, virtuous warrior. He was often shown as kind to those around him and honorable, but was also shown to be naive.{{rp|67,105}} Legends dealing with Yoshitsune's childhood show young Yoshitsune (or Ushiwakamaru) with heroic qualities. He is portrayed as a brave and skilled swordsman, despite being a young boy. He was also skilled in music and his studies, and was also said to be able to easily sway the hearts of young women. These legends delve into fantasy more so than the legends about his later life. Legends which pertain to the time when his half-brother, Yoritomo, turned against him take away some of Yoshitsune's heroic qualities. He is no longer portrayed as a great warrior, but he retains his knowledge and skills that are valuable in the emperor's court. Yoshitsune's escape through the Ataka barrier is the subject of [[:en:Noh|Noh]] play ''[[:en:Ataka (play)|Ataka]]'' and the [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]''.{{rp|89–93}} ''Kanjinchō'' was later dramatized by [[:en:Akira Kurosawa|Akira Kurosawa]] in the 1945 movie ''[[:en:The Men Who Tread on the Tiger's Tail|The Men Who Tread on the Tiger's Tail]]''. The ''[[:en:Gikeiki|Gikeiki]]'', or "''Chronicle of Yoshitsune''" relates events of Yoshitsune's life after the defeat of the Heike.{{rp|93–100}} ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshitomo|Minamoto no Yoshitomo]] * Mother: [[Tokiwa Gozen]] * Wife: Sato Gozen (1168–1189) * Concubine: [[Shizuka Gozen]] == Traditional arts == In addition to [[The Tale of the Heike]] and ''Gikeiki'', a great many other works of literature and drama feature him, and together form the ''[[sekai and shukō|sekai]]'' ("world") of Yoshitsune, a concept akin to the notion of the [[:en:literary cycle|literary cycle]]. These include: * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi|Yoshitsune Shin Takadachi]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'') * ''[[:en:Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura|Yoshitsune Senbon Zakura]]'' (''[[:en:Bunraku|jōruri]]'' and [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) * ''[[:en:Kanjinchō|Kanjinchō]]'' ([[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]]) In the visual arts, Yoshitsune is commonly depicted as a ''[[:en:Bishōnen|Bishōnen]]'', though this is at odds with contemporary descriptions of his appearance. == See also == {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Minamoto no Yoshitsune}} * [[:en:Benkei|Benkei]] * [[:en:Kurama-tengu|Kurama-tengu]] * [[:en:Kurozuka (novel)|''Kurozuka'' (novel)]] * [[:en:Letter from Koshigoe|Letter from Koshigoe]]{{rp|139}} * ''[[:en:Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II|Mysteries of Yoshitsune I&II]]'' * [[:en:Seiwa Genji|Seiwa Genji]] == References == {{Reflist}} == Further reading == * [https://www.illuminationsfantastic.com/the-song-of-yoshitsune-a-story-of-the-gempei-war-duel-at-gojo-bridge-by-alex-j-taylor-japanese-heroes-legend-history-epic-poetry-fantasy-poem-fiction-2021-illuminations-of-the-fantastic-magazine Taylor, Alex J. "The Song of Yoshitsune." Illuminations of the Fantastic Online Magazine. Poetry.] == External links == * [https://web.archive.org/web/20101017230019/http://www.samurai-archives.com/yoshitsune.html Biographical Summary] * {{Cite NIE|wstitle=Minamoto Yoshitsune|year=1905 |short=x}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1150s births]] [[Category:1189 deaths]] [[Category:Deified Japanese men]] [[Category:Imperial House of Japan]] [[Category:Japanese folklore]] [[Category:Japanese legends]] [[Category:Japanese nobility]] [[Category:Kabuki characters]] [[Category:Minamoto clan|Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Nobility from Kyoto]] [[Category:People of Heian-period Japan]] [[Category:People of Kamakura-period Japan]] [[Category:People of the Genpei War]] [[Category:Samurai]] [[Category:Suicides by seppuku]] }} [[sn:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[en:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[ar:ميناموتو نو يوشي-تسونه]] [[br:Minamoto no Yoshitune]] [[ca:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[cs:Jošicune Minamoto]] [[de:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[el:Μιναμότο Γιοσιτσούνε]] [[es:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[eu:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fa:میناموتو نو یوشی‌تسونه]] [[fi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[fr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[he:מינאמוטו נו יושיצונה]] [[hu:Minamoto no Josicune]] [[hy:Մինամոտո նո Յոշիցունե]] [[id:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[it:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ja:源義経]] [[jv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ko:미나모토노 요시쓰네]] [[lt:Minamoto no Jošicunė]] [[nl:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[pl:Yoshitsune Minamoto]] [[pt:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[ru:Минамото-но Ёсицунэ]] [[sq:Minamoto no Joshitsune]] [[sv:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[th:มินาโมโตะ โนะ โยชิตสึเนะ]] [[tr:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[uk:Мінамото-но Йосіцуне]] [[vi:Minamoto no Yoshitsune]] [[wuu:源義經]] [[zh:源義經]] [[zh-min-nan:Minamoto no Yositune]] [[zh-yue:源義經]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]]
